title: $31bn test for PM’s green grid decree
full_text:
A Singapore rival to AirTrunk has lodged a $31bn plan for Australia’s largest data centre, with the Queensland project set to challenge Anthony Albanese’s strict renewable-only rules by using gas for power generation as the state rejects the federal government’s green decree.
Zerra DC, the Stonepeak-backed offshoot of Singapore investor AGP, will build a 2.2 gigawatt AI factory in Queensland’s Western Downs region as it seeks to attract the world’s largest hyperscalers to the state, with NSW and Victoria dominating the nation’s data centre pipeline.
While the facility aims to tap into a giant 5.4GW array of renewable energy supplies in the state’s Western Downs, a first stage may be fuelled by gas with a giant battery system only to follow in a later part of the project.
Three major gas power plants are located less than 2km from the site, with Zerra still to execute procurement, generation and contracting deals. A gas well may be located on site to supply energy for the first phase of the project, according to planning documents.
Relying on fossil fuels rather than renewable energy would put Zerra DC at odds with the Prime Minister’s ambitious draft rule for all new data centres to be sourced with enough solar, wind and batteries to cover their entire demand load.
It also looms as a project that underlines how Queensland can attract enormous investment to compete with its southern rivals by allowing developers to tap into the state’s hefty gas reserves, along with its renewable resources.
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli is preparing for a scrap at this week’s national cabinet meeting on AI, where his state and the Northern Territory are the only holdouts to the federal government’s decree for the $150bn data centre industry to be fuelled entirely by renewable power.
The divide may trigger a fractious fight over the renewable rules with the Albanese government considering using constitutional powers to override Queensland’s objections to the proposed federal clampdown.
However, Queensland Energy Minister David Janetzki said federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen’s insistence to only use renewables was pure ideology.
“The truth is if you get that energy mix right you can actually complement and bring on opportunities like gas peakers, for example, that actually add to the energy mix and will give the competitive advantage to be able to get a project over the line,” Mr Janetzki said on Monday.
Zerra expects to meet both state and federal rules, saying its overall energy mix needs to reflect the region’s infrastructure, including existing generation sources such as gas.
The Business Council of Australia has previously pushed back against rules forcing data centres to power their operations with new renewable energy sources, saying gas must be part of the energy mix while warning technology mandates may hike costs.
While data centre electricity consumption is forecast to grow from around 3 per cent to 13 per cent of total electricity supply by 2035-36, the grid operator has cautioned that operating facilities used just over a quarter of available volumes, with factories taking up to a decade to reach full capacity.
Zerra is also active in other parts of Australia and has lodged plans in Melbourne to convert part of the former Ford Factory in Broadmeadows into a data centre.
That proposed facility targets cloud, AI, and other data-intensive services, involving a $6bn investment over six stages to achieve a capacity of 340 megawatts.
However, that plan has sparked a backlash from the local community about excessive noise, potential pollution, and the replacement of a manufacturing hub with a data centre.
Getting the two facilities going would make Zerra one of the largest data centre operator, positioning the company to serve hyper-scale companies with huge AI-driven requirements. Zerra is developing and operating hyperscale data centre campuses in Japan and India and is led by chief executive Dave Cooper.
Senior executives have experience from Microsoft, AWS, Google, Digital Edge DC, Vantage and AirTrunk.
Zerra is backed by independently owned global investor and asset manager AGP, which finances, develops and operates sustainable assets across energy, digital and real estate.
Zerra is also locked in a court stoush against AirTrunk, which has accused it of intellectual property breaches, with a Federal Court hearing set for September 16.
Western Downs Regional Council mayor Andrew Smith said Mr Crisafulli recommended Zerra locate its project in the area given its billing as the energy capital of the state. “We understand there’s a bit of a feel about data centres right across the nation … but without commenting on this project, it’s quite clear to anybody that has much to do with the Western Downs realises that we are a region that looks for opportunity,” Mr Smith said.
